Many essential food items are experiencing upward price pressure amid ongoing inflationary trends.

the_story: Food inflation (the rising cost of food) in India is projected to stay elevated in the coming months.
This price pressure is being caused by a shortfall in crops, a weak monsoon (seasonal rains), and high energy prices.

ICICI Bank anticipates that the Reserve Bank of India will raise interest rates by 25 basis points (0.25 percentage points) in December to manage this retail inflation (prices paid by everyday consumers).
analysis.what_happened: Food prices are staying high because bad weather and weak crop yields mean there is less food available to buy. To stop these high prices from spreading through the whole economy, banks like ICICI expect the Reserve Bank of India to step in and raise interest rates.
analysis.analogy: It is like a parent hiding the cookie jar and raising the allowance rules because the kids are eating too fast and running out of snacks—everything gets tighter to slow down the spending.
why_it_matters_india: Crop shortfalls and weak monsoons drive up food prices in local markets.
Higher food prices push up overall retail inflation across the country.
To cool down this inflation, the Reserve Bank of India is expected to raise its policy interest rate by 25 basis points.
When the central bank raises rates, commercial banks make loans and EMIs costlier for regular people.

impacts.rationale: High food prices and energy costs keep general price levels elevated, which is bad for household budgets.

impacts.target: Loan and EMI costs (home, auto, personal loans)
impacts.rationale: If the central bank raises interest rates, banks pass those costs on to borrowers, meaning higher monthly payments—generally bad for anyone with a loan.

events.headline: How India’s lithium-ion battery black mass export ban aims to reduce dependence on China for critical minerals

items.title: How India’s lithium-ion battery black mass export ban aims to reduce dependence on China for critical minerals
items.summary: India has banned lithium-ion battery black mass exports to retain critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel for domestic recycling. The move aims to strengthen local processing capacity, reduce import dependence on China, and support battery manufacturing.

events.article_text:
India has prohibited the export of lithium-ion battery black mass in a move aimed at retaining valuable critical minerals within the country, strengthening domestic recycling capabilities and reducing dependence on imports, particularly from China. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), under the Ministry of Commerce, amended the export policy for lithium-ion battery black mass from 'Free' to 'Prohibited' with immediate effect through Notification No. 49/2026-27, dated 10 November 2026. The government said the decision would ensure that battery waste generated in India is recycled and refined domestically rather than exported. The move comes as India seeks to secure supplies of critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, which are essential for electric vehicle (EV) batteries, renewable energy storage, electronics and advanced manufacturing. Black mass is a powder-like material recovered by shredding and processing discarded lithium-ion batteries and battery manufacturing waste. It contains valuable minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, which can be extracted and reused in battery production. Recycling black mass offers an alternative source of critical minerals, reducing the need for fresh mining and dependence on imported raw materials. It is particularly important for India, which has limited domestic reserves of several battery minerals. The government said domestic battery recyclers and critical mineral recovery units have been unable to utilise their full processing capacity because of inadequate availability of raw materials. Despite the expansion of India's recycling infrastructure, black mass generated domestically has continued to flow overseas. In some instances, Indian recyclers have also had to import the material to meet their requirements. The export prohibition seeks to address this mismatch by ensuring that domestically generated black mass remains available to Indian recycling and refining companies. China has a dominant position in global critical mineral supply chains, particularly in processing and refining. It accounts for roughly 60% of rare earth mining, 70-90% of processing and separation, and around 94% of permanent magnet manufacturing. Its influence also extends to the processing of minerals such as lithium, cobalt and graphite, which are essential for batteries, electric vehicles and clean-energy technologies. India's dependence on imported critical minerals leaves its manufacturing industries vulnerable to supply disruptions and geopolitical tensions. By retaining black mass within the country, India aims to recover lithium, cobalt, nickel and other valuable materials from discarded batteries and develop alternative domestic sources. The ban will not immediately eliminate India's dependence on Chinese mineral supplies. However, developing domestic recycling and refining capabilities could gradually reduce this vulnerability. According to government data cited by The Indian Express, 57 lithium-ion battery recyclers are registered on the Central Pollution Control Board's (CPCB) Battery Waste Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) portal. Together, they have an annual processing capacity of 5.17 lakh metric tonnes. However, their estimated input capacity specifically for processing lithium-ion battery black mass is around 75,500 metric tonnes annually, as per the report. The government expects the export restrictions to improve feedstock availability and help domestic facilities operate more efficiently. The measure complements the ₹1,500 crore Incentive Scheme for Critical Mineral Recycling, approved by the Union Cabinet in September 2025. The scheme seeks to develop recycling capacity to recover critical minerals from secondary sources, including battery waste and electronic waste. It also supports the National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM), which aims to strengthen domestic mineral supply chains through exploration, processing and recycling. Separately, the government has announced a ₹2,814 crore scheme providing capital expenditure support for developing domestic critical mineral processing capabilities, including lithium and nickel processing. As demand for EVs, renewable energy storage and advanced electronics rises, securing battery mineral supplies has become an economic and strategic priority. Recycling supports 'urban mining', which involves recovering valuable resources from discarded products and industrial waste instead of relying entirely on fresh mining. For India, retaining black mass could help establish a circular economy in which minerals recovered from old batteries are reused to manufacture new ones. It could also reduce dependence on overseas suppliers while supporting environmentally sound disposal and processing of hazardous battery waste. The export ban is therefore not merely a waste-management measure. It is part of India's broader effort to build strategic autonomy in critical minerals and reduce vulnerabilities in supply chains dominated by China. Bhanu Pratap is a journalist who reports and writes on foreign affairs, India’s foreign policy, geopolitics and strategic affairs. He closely follows diplomatic developments in New Delhi and has a keen interest in defence and national security.

analysis.tldr: A ban on exporting battery waste will make raw materials cheaper and more available for local recycling companies, helping build domestic EV supply chains.
the_story: The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), under the Ministry of Commerce, changed the export policy for lithium-ion battery black mass from 'Free' to 'Prohibited' with immediate effect on 10 November 2026.
Black mass is a powder recovered from discarded batteries and manufacturing waste that contains valuable critical minerals like lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese.

India has 57 registered recyclers with a total processing capacity of 5.17 lakh metric tonnes annually, but they have lacked sufficient raw materials because much of the domestic black mass was shipped overseas.
China dominates global critical mineral supply chains, controlling roughly 60% of rare earth mining, 70-90% of processing, and 94% of permanent magnet manufacturing.
The export ban complements the ₹1,500 crore Incentive Scheme for Critical Mineral Recycling approved in September 2025 and a ₹2,814 crore capital expenditure scheme for processing capabilities.
analysis.what_happened: The Indian government banned the export of lithium-ion battery black mass to keep valuable critical minerals inside the country. This happened because local recycling plants were starved of raw materials while domestic waste flowed overseas, even forcing some Indian recyclers to import the material.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local flour mill sitting empty because farmers are selling all their wheat to buyers abroad, so the government bans wheat exports to ensure the local millers have enough grain to grind.
why_it_matters_india: Domestic recyclers receive a steady, guaranteed supply of black mass instead of it being exported.
Local extraction of lithium, nickel, and cobalt increases, reducing reliance on raw material imports from dominant suppliers like China.
Lower input costs and better plant utilization improve the financial health of domestic recycling and clean-energy companies.
India builds strategic autonomy in green technologies, supporting the growth of electric vehicles (EVs) and renewable energy storage.

impacts.target: EV and clean-energy component stocks in India
impacts.rationale: secure domestic supply of critical minerals lowers input risks for local manufacturers — generally good for the sector's long-term growth.

impacts.target: India's import bill for critical minerals
impacts.rationale: recycling more waste locally reduces the need to buy expensive raw materials from abroad — good for the country's trade balance.

analysis.tldr: When global investors panic and pull money out of risky assets like Bitcoin, it can trigger wider nervous moods in global markets that eventually ripple into Indian stocks.
the_story: Bitcoin liquidation events (when exchanges automatically sell a trader's holdings because they cannot cover their losses) exceeding $500 million have become common.
Recent trading sessions saw a massive $1.3 billion liquidation.
The market is being affected by high oil prices and potential Federal Reserve (the US central bank) rate hikes (increases in borrowing costs).
Investors are currently favoring artificial intelligence stocks over cryptocurrencies during a tech selloff (a sudden, sharp drop in stock prices).
analysis.what_happened: Cryptocurrency markets have suffered massive crashes called liquidations, where traders lose over $500 million to $1.3 billion at a time. This happens because global investors are rattled by high oil prices and fears that the US Federal Reserve might raise interest rates, while also shifting their money away from crypto and into artificial intelligence tech stocks.
analysis.analogy: It is like a crowded game of musical chairs where everyone suddenly panics at the same time, drops what they are holding, and rushes toward a different, safer corner of the room.
why_it_matters_india: Global risk appetite drops -> investors sell speculative assets like crypto and tech.
Fears of US Federal Reserve rate hikes -> global money moves toward safe US assets.
International investors pull cash out of emerging markets -> creates cautious sentiment in Indian stock markets.
High global oil prices -> increases India's import costs, putting pressure on the rupee and inflation.

impacts.rationale: Global risk-off moods can occasionally spill over, making foreign investors cautious in India — generally bad for local stock portfolios.
High global oil prices and US rate hike fears strengthen the dollar, which weakens the rupee — making imported items like crude oil costlier for India.

items.title: Iraq’s Oil Production Soars to 2019 High as Hormuz Flows Surge

events.article_text:
Trump Extends Jones Act Waiver For Another 90 Days

Iraq’s crude oil production hit 4.6 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, the highest since 2019, data from the International Energy Agency’s monthly report showed on Friday, as OPEC’s second-largest producer hiked output by 540,000 bpd from September.

Kuwait and Saudi Arabia also boosted their October crude oil output compared to September, as rising volumes of oil are leaving the Strait of Hormuz on smaller tankers, which then transfer the crude cargoes onto supertankers in the Gulf of Oman.

Iraq’s October crude oil production topped its OPEC+ quota by about 170,000 bpd, showed the data in the IEA’s Oil Market Report for November.

Kuwait also boosted its crude oil production last month, from 1.58 million bpd in September to 2.03 million bpd in October, although the Gulf producer was still about 650,000 bpd short of its OPEC+ ceiling.

OPEC’s top producer and de facto leader, Saudi Arabia, hiked crude oil production by about 1 million bpd to 9.99 million bpd, up from 8.93 million bpd in September, according to IEA data.

Per the agency’s estimates, Saudi Arabia was still producing 480,000 bpd below its OPEC+ quota in October.

The Kingdom told OPEC that it pumped 10.563 million bpd in October, back near pre-war levels and slightly above its OPEC+ quota of about 10.5 million bpd. The Saudis, however, noted in OPEC’s monthly report that part of the jump in output went straight into storage, which means Saudi supply to the market for exports didn’t soar as much as production did.

Saudi Arabia’s supply to the market (domestic and overseas) was 7.122 million bpd in August, 7.988 million bpd in September, and 9.2 million bpd in October, while production was 6.238 million bpd in August, rising to 8.372 million bpd in September, and to 10.563 million bpd in October.

Gulf producers have ramped up crude oil production in recent weeks as crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have significantly increased since August, thanks to shuttle shipments through the chokepoint.

analysis.tldr: More oil coming out of the Middle East means global oil prices could drop, which usually brings down fuel costs and inflation back home in India.
the_story: Iraq's crude oil production hit 4.6 million barrels per day in October, reaching its highest level since 2019, according to International Energy Agency data.
Saudi Arabia hiked its production by about 1 million barrels per day to 9.99 million barrels per day in October.
Kuwait also boosted its production from 1.58 million barrels per day in September to 2.03 million barrels per day in October.
This jump in output happened because more oil successfully moved through the Strait of Hormuz using smaller tankers that transferred cargoes onto supertankers.
analysis.what_happened: Major Middle Eastern countries like Iraq, Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait significantly increased the amount of crude oil they produced in October. This happened because oil shipments through a vital trade route called the Strait of Hormuz improved, allowing producers to pump more oil and move it out using smaller tankers.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major water pipeline that was partially blocked suddenly getting cleared up, allowing all the water reservoirs to open their taps fully and flood the market with cheap water.
why_it_matters_india: Middle Eastern countries produce more oil and push more volume through the Strait of Hormuz.
Global crude oil supply increases, which pushes international crude oil prices down.
India imports most of its oil, so cheaper global crude means it costs less for India to buy fuel from abroad.
Lower import costs help keep inflation (general rise in prices) down and support the Indian rupee (the currency of India) against the US dollar.

impacts.rationale: More oil supply hitting the market generally pushes prices down, which is good for everyday consumers as it lowers energy costs.
When oil imports cost less, India needs fewer dollars to buy energy, which helps strengthen the rupee — good for anyone buying imported goods.
Cheaper oil lowers transport and manufacturing costs across the economy, keeping everyday prices stable for households.

events.headline: How This Year's Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger

items.title: How This Year's Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger
items.summary: A monster El Niño is nearing its peak, deepening drought in many parts of the world. Coming as countries slash foreign aid and war chokes supplies of energy and fertilizer, the climate phenomenon could leave millions more people in vulnerable countries without enough to eat. Read more on E360 →

events.article_text:
The world is now in the grip of a super El Niño: a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought. But the global organizations that keep an eye on food security are warning of even tougher times ahead.

The impacts of an El Niño can be far reaching and catastrophic. In the late 19th century, one of the strongest El Niños on record helped to fuel multiyear droughts across Asia, Brazil, and Africa that spurred a global famine: Some 50 million people, or 3 percent of the global population, died. Thankfully, the ways we plan for bad weather and move food around the planet have improved massively since then, with organizations working hard to provide relief where it’s needed. But the impacts of bad weather on crops are still hard to avoid. After a strong El Niño hit in 2015, cereal yields across Southern Africa were 20 percent below normal; crop yields in parts of Ethiopia dropped by 90 percent.

This year’s El Niño has already, by one measure, topped those previous record holders in strength. And it’s still growing. By the time the phenomenon peaks in early winter, sea-surface warming in the tropical Pacific could be higher than anything seen in a millennium. In August, the World Food Programme warned that this El Niño might push an additional 49 million people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, taking the total number to 274 million. Worryingly, this year’s event comes as global aid dollars are pinched and wars are making it hard to plug holes in global food systems.

“It’s a triple whammy of high fertilizer costs, high energy costs, and now massive droughts across the tropics,” says Berkeley Earth climatologist Zeke Hausfather, who is watching the situation unfold. “It’s not a great story.” The El Niño is one phase of a natural climate pattern called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, which has a dramatic impact on global rainfall patterns. El Niño years are marked by unusually warm waters in the tropical Pacific, which weaken winds across that patch and alter global patterns of rising and falling air pressure. The results are complicated and variable, but they tend to bring dry conditions to some tropical areas — including the Amazon and parts of Australia and Africa — and rain to other places, including Florida. The other side of the oscillation, La Niña, is marked by cooler ocean temperatures and a different pattern of wet and dry. The planet swings between the two in irregular intervals of years, sometimes with neutral periods in between.

Both sides of this cycle can harm crops, though one prominent 2014 study found that El Niño affects a larger swath of the globe’s harvested land. While some places get more water, and some crops thrive, in many spots drought withers production. That same study found that an El Niño tends to improve global soybean production by up to 5 percent but suppresses maize, rice, and wheat by up to 4 percent. The numbers in any one country can be much more dramatic than that: Since 1980, South Africa’s maize output, for example, has averaged about 28 percent below normal during El Niño years.

Cereal disruptions, even if small, can hit hard if they come on top of other economic strains, says Stanford agricultural economist David Lobell. “When markets are tight, then if there’s a drought somewhere, that’s a much bigger deal.”

And the markets are, indeed, tight. Global average food prices have been trending upwards for about 20 years, says Lobell, thanks to climate blows stacking on top of each other. And this year has brought additional strains. When the U.S. and Israel launched an attack on Iran at the end of February, marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz ground to a near halt for months. The transport of oil was choked, energy prices spiked, and the supply of fertilizer, which is most often made with hydrogen sourced from cheap natural gas, was severely pinched: The Middle East usually produces a quarter of the world’s fertilizer. Meanwhile, the ongoing war in Ukraine continues to play havoc with the cost of fuel and restrict the transport of wheat from a major hub on the Black Sea.

As of October, the warming in the mid-tropical Pacific that’s used to measure the strength of an El Niño hit 3.5 degrees C — breaking the previous record of about 2.75 degrees C — and is on its way to an unprecedented peak of around 4 degrees C, according to Hausfather. “That’s scary,” he says. Broadly speaking, he says, the more powerful the El Niño, the more powerful its effects on weather events, including droughts.

Unusually, this year’s El Niño is the third “strong” El Niño event to hit within a relatively short span of 11 years, which means some areas have been hit repeatedly with drought. The higher-than-usual frequency of El Niños may itself be caused by climate change, some researchers have suggested — though this is still an area of hot debate, Hausfather says.

All these factors act together, with cascading impacts that can take months to develop and last for years. “The confluence of drought and conflict drives some of the worst outcomes we see,” says Richard Choularton, director of climate and resilience for the World Food Programme in Rome. A farmer can’t afford fertilizer; then his fields face drought. In anticipation of a bad year, he plants less and hires fewer people. The river used to transport his crop dries up, and the port that takes it overseas has been bombed out of commission. His cows have little to eat. A year later, he can’t afford to buy groceries or fuel his farming equipment. The lack of rain allows seawater to seep into aquifers, so fresh water gets rationed. Hydropower plants sputter. And on it goes.

While any year brings its own spates of bad weather — some of it random, and some made more likely by the pressures of climate change — plenty of events this year have been attributed to the El Niño. Among the first to be hit was the

analysis.tldr: A severe global climate pattern combined with fertilizer shortages and wars means food and farming costs are likely to stay high, making household grocery budgets tighter.
the_story: The world is experiencing a super El Niño—a massive warming of ocean waters in the tropical Pacific—with warming hitting 3.5 degrees Celsius in October and heading toward an unprecedented 4 degrees C peak.
The World Food Programme warned that this phenomenon could push an additional 49 million people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027.
Global food production faces a triple whammy of high fertilizer costs, high energy costs, and severe droughts across the tropics.

Attacks involving Iran and the U.S. choked marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, pinching the supply of fertilizer (the Middle East produces a quarter of the world's fertilizer), while the war in Ukraine continues to disrupt wheat and fuel transport.
analysis.what_happened: A natural climate cycle called El Niño has caused record-breaking ocean warming in the Pacific, disrupting global weather, shrinking rivers, and causing droughts. This is hitting the world at a time when global food markets are already strained by high energy costs, expensive fertilizers, and wars.
analysis.analogy: It is like a restaurant suffering from a drought that ruins its vegetable supply, while at the same time its gas and cooking oil bills double because of a delivery strike outside—forcing the owner to raise menu prices just to survive.
why_it_matters_india: Middle East conflicts and halted marine traffic choke the global supply of fertilizer, which is often made from natural gas.
Because India imports a large share of its fertilizer, global supply pinches push up import costs.
Higher input costs and weather disruptions lead to lower crop yields (such as maize, rice, and wheat) or higher costs to grow them.
These agricultural strains feed into higher domestic food inflation, meaning ordinary families pay more for everyday groceries.

impacts.rationale: Global droughts and high farming costs lead to scarcer crops and higher prices—bad for ordinary households buying groceries.

impacts.target: Fertilizer subsidy costs for the Indian government
impacts.rationale: Squeezed global fertilizer supplies from Middle East disruptions push up import costs, forcing the government to spend more to keep prices affordable for farmers.

events.headline: Why the Arctic cannot replace the Middle East’s shipping lanes

items.title: Why the Arctic cannot replace the Middle East’s shipping lanes
items.summary: Russian Arctic energy, not Arctic shipping, is the real beneficiary of the current crisis – and Western sanctions complicate even that.

events.article_text:
The nuclear icebreaker Yakutia designed to ensure shipping in the Arctic and support the development of the Northern Sea Route (Artem Priakhin via Getty Images)

Russian Arctic energy, not Arctic shipping, is the real beneficiary of the current crisis – and Western sanctions complicate even that.

Why the Arctic cannot replace the Middle East’s shipping lanes

The war involving Iran, Israel and the United States has severely disrupted (Opens in new window)shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while renewed Houthi attacks have made the Bab el-Mandeb Strait more dangerous. With two of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints under pressure, shipping companies are looking for alternatives. One possibility is the Northern Sea Route (NSR), which runs along Russia’s Arctic coastline.

Climate change has made Arctic waters more accessible, raising hopes that the NSR could offer a shorter connection between Europe and East Asia. However, the route’s geographical, economic and political limitations make it an unlikely substitute for Middle Eastern shipping corridors. During the Arctic sailing season, the NSR handles fewer than 0.5% (Opens in new window) as many weekly vessel transits between East Asia and Europe (Opens in new window) as conventional routes. Its greatest potential contribution to the current crisis may instead come from Russian Arctic energy exports.

The NSR offers substantial distance savings (Opens in new window) for some voyages between northern Europe and Northeast Asia. Yet a shorter route does not necessarily translate into lower costs. Ice conditions restrict navigation, particularly during winter, while vessels may require ice-class capabilities or icebreaker assistance. Russia also imposes navigation requirements and charges, adding costs (Opens in new window) and administrative complications.

Environmental and operational risks (Opens in new window) present further obstacles. Arctic waters have limited search-and-rescue infrastructure, while an oil spill in remote, ice-covered waters would be exceptionally difficult to contain. These risks increase the importance of insurance, emergency preparedness and specialised vessels. Western sanctions against Russia introduce financial and legal complications.

Production and shipping constraints limit these projects’ immediate contribution, while redirecting existing exports would do little to increase global supply.

Geography also limits (Opens in new window) the NSR’s usefulness. Although the route can accommodate some large vessels, ice conditions, navigational restrictions and limited infrastructure constrain its capacity to handle the enormous volumes carried through conventional shipping corridors. Furthermore, the NSR primarily benefits trade between Europe and Northeast Asia. It offers little advantage for shipments originating in the Persian Gulf or travelling between Asia and destinations outside northern Europe.

For most shipping companies, diverting vessels around the Cape of Good Hope remains a more practical (Opens in new window) response to disruptions in the Red Sea. However, this diversion cannot circumvent the Strait of Hormuz for cargo originating inside the Persian Gulf. Although this adds distance and fuel costs, the route accommodates the world’s largest commercial vessels and operates year-round without Arctic ice restrictions.

Nevertheless, the Arctic could provide some relief through energy production rather than container shipping. Russian Arctic hydrocarbons could reach Asian consumers without passing through Hormuz or Bab el-Mandeb.

Russia’s Vostok Oil project began exports in September 2026 (Opens in new window), while the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project has demonstrated (Opens in new window) its ability to produce LNG despite logistical difficulties. Both projects could eventually contribute additional hydrocarbons to international markets, reducing dependence on supplies passing through Middle Eastern chokepoints. However, production and shipping constraints limit these projects’ immediate contribution, while redirecting existing exports would do little to increase global output.

Expanding these projects would also present Western governments with an uncomfortable choice: whether improving energy security justifies relaxing sanctions that constrain Russia’s ability to finance its war against Ukraine.

China is particularly well positioned (Opens in new window) to benefit from growing Russian Arctic energy exports, having invested in Arctic energy projects and participated in NSR shipping. Japan also has investments (Opens in new window) in Russian LNG developments, while South Korea (Opens in new window) and India (Opens in new window) have explored Arctic maritime opportunities. However, sanctions and political considerations complicate their participation, particularly for US allies Japan and South Korea.

The Middle East crisis is unlikely to turn the Arctic into an alternative Suez Canal. Instead, it may reinforce a different development: the importance of Russian Arctic energy to Asian markets, even as Western sanctions limit the region’s potential.

Paul Weisko is a researcher at the Israel-China Policy Center at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) in Tel Aviv and a PhD student in Political Science at the University of Haifa.

analysis.tldr: Middle East shipping disruptions will keep oil transport costs and fuel prices elevated for India, as icy Arctic routes cannot step in to replace traditional sea lanes.
the_story: Conflicts involving Iran, Israel, and the US have severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while Houthi attacks have made the Bab el-Mandeb Strait dangerous.

The Northern Sea Route (NSR) along Russia's Arctic coastline is being looked at as an alternative, but it handles fewer than 0.5% as many weekly vessel transits as conventional routes during its sailing season.

Arctic shipping faces severe limits due to ice conditions, high costs for icebreaker assistance, strict Russian navigation charges, and the risks of operating in remote waters without proper rescue infrastructure.

Instead of container shipping, the Arctic's main contribution during the crisis may be Russian Arctic energy exports like the Vostok Oil project and Arctic LNG 2 reaching Asian consumers without passing through Middle Eastern chokepoints.
analysis.what_happened: Middle East conflicts and attacks have blocked major shipping lanes, forcing companies to seek alternatives. While people hope the Arctic's Northern Sea Route can help, harsh ice, high costs, and geography make it impossible to replace traditional routes. As a result, ships continue to take longer detours around Africa, keeping transport and energy costs high.
analysis.analogy: It is like trying to reroute highway traffic through a narrow, freezing mountain trail packed with snow: it sounds shorter on a map, but in reality, it is too dangerous, slow, and expensive to carry heavy trucks.
why_it_matters_india: Middle East maritime chokepoints face ongoing security pressures, preventing easy maritime shortcuts through the Arctic.
Global shipping companies rely on longer detours like the Cape of Good Hope, raising fuel and freight transport costs.
Higher transport and regional energy supply strains keep global crude oil and energy prices elevated.
As a major energy importer, higher global crude costs translate to costlier imports for India, impacting domestic fuel prices and macro stability.

impacts.rationale: Persistent Middle East shipping blockades and costly detours keep global oil supply expenses high, which is bad for everyday consumers at the pump.
Costlier fuel and transport expenses filter through the economy to make everyday goods and services more expensive — bad for household budgets.
Higher import bills for crude oil mean India needs more dollars to pay for energy, which tends to weaken the local currency — bad for purchasing power.

watch_next: Security developments in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Strait
Updates on Russian Arctic energy production and exports reaching Asian markets
analysis.caveats: If a sudden diplomatic breakthrough ends the Middle East conflicts, shipping lanes could reopen quickly and lower transport costs.

events.headline: How Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia impacts China’s AI supply chain

items.title: How Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia impacts China’s AI supply chain
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang attends a summit at the Institute of Peace on October 8, 2026 in Washington, DC.

events.article_text:
Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, days after he admitted to having an affair with a Chinese data center executive, whom the U.S. intelligence agency believed to be a Chinese government agent. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive.

Nvidia’s board said that chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as the company’s interim chief executive until a permanent successor has been named.

Huang’s exit has triggered worries about Nvidia’s future as the world’s top chipmaker, and about the entire AI industry where Nvidia has been a hardware provider, an investor, and a community leader. Repercussions from the saga will impact China, which has yet to replace Nvidia chips with domestic alternatives, as well as Taiwan and South Korea, which host a vast network of Nvidia suppliers.

Here are the key questions emerging from Huang’s dramatic downfall.

Jensen Huang had been the biggest advocate for selling chips to China, which he argued helps America maintain its market dominance.

Despite the U.S. banning the export of advanced Nvidia chips to China, Chinese companies have been trying to access chips remotely by working with data centers in Southeast Asia.

Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang had an affair, served as the executive of Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia. The Information reported that Alice Huang helped move about 240,000 H100, H200 and some A100 chips into China. Her companies also invested in DeepSeek, promising to supply Nvidia chips.

The Nvidia scandal will likely lead the U.S. government to tighten chip controls. Anticipating a crackdown, Chinese AI labs are trying to lock in overseas supplies of Nvidia chips, while traders in China are stockpiling restricted chips, Reuters reported.

Chinese chips are catching up in performance, but Nvidia chips are still essential to the AI industry.

In the first half of the year, Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China, down 44% from a year earlier and making up 34% of the market, according to a Reuters report, citing IDC data. In the same period, leading Chinese chipmaker HuaweiiHuaweiHuawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions.READ MORE shipped 572,000 ‌AI ⁠accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, accounting for 28% of the market,

AlibabaiAlibabaAlibaba, founded in 1999 by Chinese entrepreneur Jack Ma, is one of the most prominent global e-commerce companies that operates platforms like AliExpress, Taobao, and Tmall.READ MORE’s chip unit T-Head had 7% of the market, followed by Cambricon’s 5%. BaiduiBaiduBaidu is a Chinese technology company that operates the country’s biggest search engine and video-streaming service iQiyi.READ MORE subsidiary Kunlunxin held 4% and Hygon had 3%.

Although AI labs are increasingly working with chipmakers to make sure their models can run on domestic infrastructure, most AI developers still train new models on Nvidia chips. Nvidia’s B300 delivers 6.75 times the arithmetic performance of Huawei’s best Ascend 950 chip, according to research firm Epoch AI. Huawei also lags behind Nvidia in production volume.

Jensen Huang enjoys rock star status across Asia, especially in his birth country Taiwan, where he would visit night markets, share snacks with fans, and host banquets with executives of Taiwanese suppliers. He said the company planned to invest $150 billion a year in Taiwan.

Many internet users expressed disappointment that they lost a role model in tech. Some wrote that the spy allegations and the criticisms of Huang would add to the discrimination of Asians working in America’s tech industry.

Huang’s departure is also creating uncertainty around Nvidia’s supply chain relationship with Asian companies. But several executives at Nvidia’s Taiwanese suppliers said they still expected steady orders from Nvidia in the coming years because of the sustained demand from the AI industry, according to Taiwan’s Central News Agency.

In her new book “Reboot: AI and the Race to Save Democracy,” writer Beth Simone Noveck warns that while AI can increase efficiency, predictive models pose significant ethical and societal risks.

Labor disputes and unionization in Taiwan’s semiconductor industry highlight growing worker discontent over the unequal distribution of profits from the AI boom.

A growing number of startups are editing powerful Chinese open-weight models for Western businesses that are concerned about censorship and security.

analysis.tldr: Nvidia's boss stepping down could lead the US to strictly block AI chips from reaching China, creating a ripple effect on global tech stocks that Indian tech companies and investors closely track.
the_story: Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after admitting to an affair with a Chinese data center executive linked to US intelligence as a government agent.
Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim chief executive while the board searches for a permanent successor.
Reports showed that Alice Huang, the executive involved, helped move roughly 240,000 advanced Nvidia chips into China via Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed.
In the first half of the year, Nvidia's shipments in China fell 44% to 678,000 units (making up 34% of the market), while Chinese rival Huawei shipped 572,000 units.
Executives at Nvidia's Taiwanese suppliers expect steady future orders despite the leadership change due to massive, ongoing global demand for artificial intelligence hardware.
analysis.what_happened: Nvidia's top leader abruptly resigned following revelations about a personal relationship with a foreign data center executive who moved restricted chips into China. This sudden departure has panicked the artificial intelligence industry and raised fears that the US government will crack down harder on chip exports.
analysis.analogy: It is like the star captain of a major global shipping company stepping down overnight because of a security scandal, leaving all the clients who rely on his cargo worried about whether their packages will clear customs.
why_it_matters_india: US chip restrictions tighten -> Global tech supply chains face sudden shifts and regulatory stress.
Global tech stocks wobble -> Indian IT (Information Technology) and hardware stocks experience market jitters.
Global artificial intelligence hardware costs rise -> Developing advanced artificial intelligence models becomes more expensive for firms worldwide.

Uncertainty hits global markets -> Foreign institutional investors (FIIs [big foreign investors investing from outside India]) adjust portfolios, affecting Indian stock indices like the Nifty 50 [India's main stock market index].

impacts.rationale: Global tech hardware disruptions and market jitters can temporarily drag down Indian technology stocks, which is generally unsettling for local equity investors.
Broader global tech sector panics sometimes spill over into Indian markets via foreign investor selling, creating short-term volatility for regular investors.

How Nvidia's interim chief executive handles existing supply contracts in Taiwan and South Korea
analysis.caveats: If Nvidia's board quickly names a stable permanent leader, market panic over supply chain disruptions could fade away rapidly.

events.headline: Potential Adverse Impact of FTAs on Public Procurement Policies Supporting Made in India

items.title: Potential Adverse Impact of FTAs on Public Procurement Policies Supporting Made in India
items.summary: As trade agreements open up public procurement to foreign suppliers, India must safeguard domestic manufacturing preferences and ensure that market access commitments bring reciprocal benefits, investment and technology transfer.

events.article_text:
Public procurement policies across government departments and public sector undertakings (PSUs) have been considerably streamlined through the adoption of the Government e-Marketplace (GeM). The platform enables manufacturers, including micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), to list products with specifications, giving public procuring entities a wider choice and helping them secure competitive prices. Reverse bidding after shortlisting also enables further price discovery.

The platform allows manufacturers and suppliers to access procurement opportunities through technology, while measures aimed at ensuring prompt payments by public entities help prevent working capital from being unnecessarily locked up. Preference for domestic suppliers and manufacturers through public procurement can strengthen local supply chains and make procurement an instrument for promoting innovation. For this, it is important that procurement specifications are outcome-based rather than unnecessarily prescriptive, allowing new technologies to find a place in actual use.

Equally important is assessing whether non-discrimination provisions in various free trade agreements (FTAs) could adversely affect domestic industries, particularly MSMEs. Sectors such as dairy and textiles may be particularly exposed. The success of the domestic procurement policy will also depend on ease of listing on GeM, flexibility in procurement specifications and timely payments by government departments and PSUs. Effective implementation can support not only manufacturing in India but also innovation.

This makes it important to examine how trade agreements could affect the government's ability to use public procurement to advance the Make in India objective. Beyond the procurement mechanism itself, another area requiring close scrutiny is the treatment of government procurement in FTAs proposed or negotiated with partners such as the European Union (EU), the US and South Korea. Past experience with reciprocity has not always been encouraging.

There are also non-trade measures, such as the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which covers steel and other materials. The imposition of a carbon-related levy can add to the cost of Indian exports. Whether revenues collected under CBAM should support Indian industries in their transition towards green steel also merits policy attention. The impact of multinational companies in the services sector should likewise be examined in terms of their implications for MSMEs.

Yet, the potential conflicts between India's FTA commitments and its Make in India objective of attracting investment and generating employment within the country rarely receive adequate attention.

The paper, EU FTA negotiations with India: The question of liberalisation of public procurement (Sangeeta Khorana and Anand N. Asthana, Asia Europe Journal, Vol. 12, No. 3, 2014), highlighted the EU's insistence on including public procurement within a non-discrimination framework. India's expanding infrastructure sector presents an opportunity for overseas suppliers to enter a growing market, where a substantial share of expenditure is undertaken by the government through public procurement of inputs.

In return, market access for services may be less durable, as services can often be sourced from other countries at lower cost and access remains subject to work-permit and visa restrictions. In 2006, the EU identified expanded access to public procurement as an objective in trade negotiations with countries with which it sought FTAs.

Past FTAs have, in some instances, produced outcomes that India regarded as adverse, with partner countries failing to provide comparable market access in areas where India had an advantage while maintaining protectionist measures of their own. India has also resorted to safeguard measures in response to surges in imports, including in trade with South Korea. These experiences underline the need to link market access to genuine reciprocity and, wherever possible, encourage investment and manufacturing partnerships in India, including in steel products such as hot-rolled coil.

There is a potential contradiction between supporting domestic manufacturing, including through preferences for Made in India products in public procurement, and accepting broad non-discrimination commitments under FTAs. If not carefully designed, such commitments could constrain domestic manufacturing and employment opportunities. This is particularly important given India's large working-age population. The services sector alone may not provide sufficient employment security, especially while a large share of the workforce remains in informal employment.

India's Preference to Make in India (PMI) policy in public procurement has supported the expansion of MSMEs, which can, in turn, stimulate investment and employment. Public procurement has therefore become a significant issue in newer trade negotiations. India's procurement market is substantial and currently includes local-preference provisions, including thresholds applicable to certain procurements.

This calls for continued caution as modern, 'new-generation' trade agreements increasingly provide for limited, transparent or reciprocal access to central-government procurement. Such provisions must be carefully drafted to ensure that they do not unintentionally erode legitimate domestic-preference policies. The India-UK trade framework, for example, illustrates the importance of examining the scope of commitments at the central-government level in sectors such as railways and energy, where India has significant manufacturing capabilities.

Sensitive domains such as space and defence require particular care. Procurement-related commitments under agreements involving EFTA countries and the UAE likewise demonstrate that public procurement, once treated as a sensitive area in trade negotiations, is increasingly becoming part of India's trade architecture.

As I

analysis.tldr: Trade deals with foreign nations could clash with government rules favoring local Indian goods, which matters for the growth of domestic manufacturing and local jobs.
the_story: India uses the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) platform to streamline public procurement, helping MSMEs (micro, small and medium enterprises) list products and secure competitive prices through reverse bidding.

Rules favoring domestic suppliers in public procurement strengthen local supply chains, but non-discrimination clauses in free trade agreements (FTAs) with partners like the EU, the US, South Korea, the UK, EFTA, and the UAE pose potential risks to domestic industries like dairy and textiles.
The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) imposes a carbon-related levy on materials like steel, which can increase the cost of Indian exports and require policy attention.
Past trade agreements have sometimes led to outcomes where partner countries maintained protectionist measures while failing to offer comparable market access in areas where India held an advantage.
analysis.what_happened: An opinion piece discusses how India's free trade agreements with global partners might conflict with the 'Make in India' goal of favoring local manufacturers in government purchases. The article highlights that as India negotiates modern trade deals, rules requiring equal treatment for foreign and domestic suppliers could limit the government's ability to support local MSMEs and domestic industries.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local grocery shop owner who promised to buy vegetables only from neighborhood farmers to help them grow, but then signed a mall partnership agreement that forces them to also consider cheaper foreign suppliers.
why_it_matters_india: Trade agreements include non-discrimination commitments that may allow foreign companies to compete for Indian government procurement contracts.
This increased foreign competition could weaken local preference policies that currently support Indian MSMEs and domestic manufacturing.
A slowdown in domestic manufacturing could impact employment generation for India's large working-age population.
Additional non-trade costs like the EU's CBAM carbon levy could raise expenses for Indian exporters in sectors like steel.

impacts.target: MSMEs and domestic manufacturing sectors like dairy & textiles
impacts.rationale: Broader FTA commitments could expose small local businesses to intense foreign competition, making it harder for them to secure government contracts.
Carbon-related levies like the EU's CBAM increase export costs, reducing competitiveness for Indian steel makers.
Potential policy friction in trade deals could create headwinds for domestic industrial and manufacturing growth.

watch_next: Progress and specific terms on public procurement in ongoing India-EU and India-UK trade negotiations
Updates on how revenues collected under the EU's CBAM are managed to support green transitions for Indian industries
analysis.caveats: Trade negotiations are complex and subject to change based on reciprocal concessions and final treaty wording.

history.title: The bubble that took thirty years to repay
history.what: At its 1989 peak the Tokyo stock market was worth more than the American one, and the land under the Imperial Palace was said to be worth more than all of California. The Nikkei then fell about 80% and did not regain its 1989 high until 2024 — thirty-five years later.
history.why: The 1985 Plaza Accord pushed the yen sharply higher, hurting exporters. The Bank of Japan cut rates hard to compensate, and the cheap money went into land and shares rather than into business investment. Banks lent against property using property as collateral, so rising prices justified more lending, which raised prices further. A closed loop, and everyone inside it could point to a rational-sounding reason.
history.impact: Households and banks spent two decades repairing balance sheets instead of spending and lending. Growth flatlined, prices actually fell for years, and a generation entered a frozen job market. Japan's share of world output fell from roughly 15% to under 5%.
history.policy: Rates went to zero and later below it. Japan invented quantitative easing in 2001 — a central bank creating money to buy government bonds — because conventional rate cuts had run out of room. Banks were eventually forced to recognise bad loans instead of rolling them over.
history.consequence: Every major central bank used Japan's playbook in 2008 and again in 2020, which is why zero rates and bond-buying stopped being exotic. Japan also proved an economy can stagnate for decades without a dramatic collapse — the danger is not always a crash.
history.pattern: When an asset is bought with debt secured against that same asset, the cycle feeds itself upward and then downward with equal force. Ask what the collateral is; if the collateral is the thing being bought, you are looking at the mechanism.
history.india_echo: Indian property lending and promoter share-pledging are the same shape on a smaller scale. It is why the RBI watches loan-to-value ratios, and why a promoter pledging shares to buy more shares deserves real suspicion.
history.watch_for: Lending growth running far ahead of income growth, with the asset itself as the security. That combination has never ended gently.
